summary: Describes tests for measuring the performance of firewalls and a standard way to report the results, so that different products can be compared fairly. It comes from the IETF Benchmarking Methodology Working Group. It is informational and was later replaced by RFC 9411.

plainLanguage.summary: A firewall is like a security guard at a door. This memo says how to time the guard fairly, such as how many people they check per minute, so different guards can be compared and the results written down the same way.

subtitle: Standard tests for measuring and comparing firewall performance.

tldr.problem: Different firewall products perform very differently, and there is no standard way to test and report their performance, making fair comparison impossible.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines a set of benchmarking tests covering throughput, connection handling, latency, denial of service resilience, and other characteristics, along with standard formats for reporting results.
tldr.outcome: It was replaced by RFC 9411 with updated methodologies.

today: RFC 3511 is Informational and has been superseded by RFC 9411 with updated benchmarking methodologies. The fundamental testing principles defined here remain foundational for firewall performance evaluation.

sections.title: Benchmarking Tests and Methodology
sections.content: Firewalls protect networks by filtering traffic based on access control policies. This document defines benchmarking tests that measure firewall performance in four areas: forwarding (how much data can pass through), connection handling (how many simultaneous connections), latency (how long data takes to cross), and filtering (how rules affect performance). The tests are based on virtual clients and servers that simulate realistic network load. Tests cover IP throughput, concurrent TCP connections, maximum connection establishment and tear-down rates, HTTP transfer rates, denial of service handling, illegal traffic filtering, IP fragmentation, and latency.
sections.plainLanguage: Tests measure how fast the firewall works, how many conversations it handles at once, how quickly requests get answered, and how well it blocks bad traffic.

sections.title: Test Configuration and Parameters
sections.content: Firewall tests use two standard configurations: dual-homed (protecting a private network from the Internet) and tri-homed (with a Demilitarized Zone for public servers). Tests specify parameters such as packet size, connection attempt rate, object size, HTTP version, and rule sets. Network Address Translation (NAT) should be tested both enabled and disabled to isolate its performance impact. Virtual clients and servers may not correspond to physical hosts; one data source can emulate multiple clients. Authentication processes must be included in measurements. TCP stack parameters must be configured identically when comparing multiple firewalls. Test duration must be sufficient (at least 30 seconds) to ensure stable measurements.
sections.plainLanguage: Tests set up realistic network conditions with specific numbers for packet sizes, traffic rates, and rules. Both simple and complex configurations are tested.

sections.title: Throughput, Connection Rates, and Latency
sections.content: IP throughput measures the maximum data rate the firewall can forward without packet loss, using an iterative search algorithm. TCP connection capacity tests find the maximum number of concurrent connections the firewall can hold in its state table. Connection establishment and tear-down tests measure the maximum rate at which new connections can be opened and closed. Denial of service handling tests measure performance under TCP SYN flood attacks, with optional SYN attack defense mechanisms enabled or disabled. Latency is measured as the delay incurred by data crossing the firewall at the throughput level (maximum load with zero loss). Both network-layer (IP/UDP) and application-layer (HTTP) latency tests are defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Tests measure raw speed, how many connections at once, how fast new connections start and stop, how the firewall handles attacks, and response time delays.

sections.title: HTTP and Application-Layer Testing
sections.content: HTTP transfer rate tests measure the throughput of application-layer data transfers, specifying the number of connections, GET requests per connection, and object sizes. HTTP transaction rate tests find the maximum sustained rate of HTTP requests and responses. Virtual clients request objects in a round-robin pattern across multiple servers. Tests must use HTTP 1.1 or higher to support persistent connections, which is important for realistic firewall benchmarking. Intermediate results are recorded as the test varies offered load to find maximum performance. Results are reported in tabular form with separate sections for application-layer and transport-layer measurements.
sections.plainLanguage: Tests measure how many web pages the firewall can download per second and how many transactions it handles at once, mimicking real web browsing.

sections.title: Illegal Traffic and IP Fragmentation
sections.content: Illegal traffic handling tests measure performance when the firewall must filter a mix of allowed and disallowed traffic based on access control rules. The test specifies what percentage of connections should be blocked and measures the firewall's ability to drop illegal traffic without affecting performance on legal traffic. IP fragmentation tests determine performance impact when packets are fragmented due to smaller MTU values on intermediate networks. Tests are performed with fragmented traffic denied, allowed, and with anti-fragmentation policies enabled. These tests help identify whether filtering rules or reassembly processing are performance bottlenecks.
sections.plainLanguage: Tests check if the firewall can reject bad traffic without slowing down good traffic, and if reassembling broken-up packets slows it down.
